claims.text: A two-phase coexistence method can be used to calculate melting properties of refractory materials.
The two-phase coexistence method is often implemented using ab initio molecular dynamics.
The method uses a simulation cell containing coexisting solid and liquid regions.
The coexistence simulation can be run with DFT-based molecular dynamics under NVE or NPT ensembles.
The simulation should be conducted near the expected melting temperature and at a pressure appropriate for the material.
The simulation cell must be large enough to sustain a stable solid-liquid interface.
The solid-liquid interface forms and evolves during the simulation.
Natural adjustment of the solid-liquid interface drives the simulated system toward equilibrium at the melting point.
Steady coexistence of solid and liquid phases identifies the melting temperature.
Properties of the coexisting phases and interface provide information from which the latent heat and volume change upon fusion can be obtained.
The coexistence simulation can determine the melting temperature, entropy of fusion, enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
Homogeneous simulations such as heating a perfect crystal require expensive thermodynamic integration.
Homogeneous simulations may not readily yield melting properties other than the melting temperature.
Finite-size effects may limit the precision of the two-phase coexistence method.
The accuracy with which DFT describes both solid and liquid phases may limit the precision of predicted melting properties.
Extracting entropy and enthalpy of fusion may be less straightforward than extracting the melting temperature.
The two-phase coexistence method is less computationally demanding than full thermodynamic integration.
The robustness of the method for accurately determining all melting properties of high-melting refractory materials has not been thoroughly validated.
